question: What does the Bible say about human nature?
intro: Christians ask what a human being is: what a person is made of (body and soul, body, soul and spirit, or one living whole), what it means that people are made in God's image, and what Adam's fall changed in those who came after him. The readings below join these three matters in different ways, and the traditions do not always line up behind one of them. This page sets the readings side by side and chooses none. How far sin reaches into the will belongs to the card on total depravity and is left there.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that God made human beings, male and female, from the ground and by his breath, in his image, and called what he made very good. The text also calls Christ the image of God. It also speaks of people as made in God's image or likeness after Adam's fall, in Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9. The Christian readings below all take the text to say that all have sinned, that death comes to all in Adam, and that life comes in Christ. They differ over what a human being is made of, how the image and likeness are to be understood, and how Adam's act reaches those who came after him.

passages.quote: So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.
Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.
And God looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good.
The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation.
for in His own image God has made mankind.
With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God's likeness.
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.

readings.label: Body and soul made in God's image and called to union with him: the fall brought death and left a corrupted or wounded nature
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the text to describe a human being as body and soul together, made in God's image and made for union with God. Some early writers named three parts, body, soul and spirit. Catholic teaching names body and soul, and takes “spirit” to be the soul in its ordering to God, not a third part (Catechism 367). Catholic teaching speaks of original sin as the loss of the holiness and justice with which Adam was made, handed on by descent as a state and not as a personal act, leaving human nature wounded and not destroyed (Catechism 399, 404-405; Council of Trent, Session 5). The Orthodox Church in America, in a reply on its teaching pages, says that the consequences of the first sin, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) speaks of hereditary sin that flowed to Adam's posterity and of infants as subject to original sin, and the Longer Catechism (Q168) says all are born infected with sin and mortal. Many writers of the Eastern Orthodox tradition take “image” and “likeness” in Genesis 1:26 as two things: the image given, and the likeness to be grown into through a life of union with God (what is called theosis). None of the Orthodox documents cited here states this; the Longer Catechism (Q114) speaks only of the image, as righteousness and holiness of truth.

passages.quote: Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness
passages.note: Image and likeness named as two words; many in this reading hear two things.

passages.quote: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
passages.note: A person named as body and soul.

passages.quote: We are confident, then, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
passages.note: Read as the person present with the Lord apart from the body.

passages.quote: Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.
passages.note: Death passed on to all through one man.

passages.quote: and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
passages.note: Read as naming the righteousness and holiness humans were made with and are given again.

passages.quote: and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.
passages.note: The image renewed in those who are in Christ.

passages.quote: And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.
passages.note: Read as the likeness the believer grows into: the heavenly man's.

passages.quote: so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.
passages.note: Read as the goal of a human life: sharing in the divine nature.

passages.quote: through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners
passages.note: The many made sinners through one man's disobedience, set beside the many made righteous through one man's obedience.

passages.quote: From one man He made every nation of men
passages.note: Every nation of men is said to be made from one man.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take 1 Thessalonians 5:23, the verse that names three, to describe the one soul in its powers, or the whole person from different sides, and not a third part; they take Hebrews 4:12, which speaks of soul and spirit as divided, to describe the whole person reached by the word. Catholic members take Psalm 51:5 and Ephesians 2:3 to speak of a state received by descent and not of a personal act; Eastern Orthodox members take them to speak of a mortal, corruptible nature in a world already marked by sin. Both take Ezekiel 18:20 to address a person's own deeds before God. Eastern Orthodox members take the clause “because all sinned” in Romans 5:12 to mean each person's own sin, with the inherited mortality named before it; Catholic members take Romans 5:12 with the whole of Paul's account to speak of all sharing in Adam's sin, handed on by descent, and the Latin text their tradition long used can be rendered 'in whom all sinned'. Catholic members commonly state the image and likeness so: the image of God kept after the fall, and the likeness, lost through original sin, restored by grace. Both take “dead in your trespasses and sins” in Ephesians 2:1 as separation from God's life that Christ restores, applied to the whole person.

readings.label: Fallen in Adam: his sin brought condemnation and a corrupted nature on all his descendants (what is called original sin)
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Romans 5 and the verses near it to say that Adam's sin brought condemnation and a corrupted nature on all who descend from him, so that each person is born under that condemnation and with that corruption. Lutheran readers, following the Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration, Article I), speak of the image as lost in its original righteousness and holiness, the person remaining God's creature. Reformed readers speak of the image as lost in the knowledge, righteousness and holiness it first had; Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 are cited for a dignity that remains in the person, which Reformed writers state as the image remaining in a lesser sense. Lutheran readers confess this in the Augsburg Confession (Article II) and the Solid Declaration. Reformed readers confess it in the Westminster Confession (chapter 6) and the Canons of Dort (Third and Fourth Heads), and add that Adam stood for the whole human family (what is called federal headship), which the Westminster Confession (7.2), held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, sets in a covenant of works made with Adam and his posterity. Reformed confessions also speak of children who die in infancy: the Canons of Dort (I.17), held by the Christian Reformed Church, say that believing parents should not doubt the election and salvation of children God takes in infancy, and the Westminster Confession (10.3) says elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved. Anglican readers hold the corruption of human nature in Article IX of the Church of England, which adds that it remains in the baptized and that every person born deserves God's wrath and damnation, with no condemnation for those who believe; Anglican members differ in how they state the guilt, and the catechism of the Anglican Church in North America (question 46) speaks of an inherited fallen and corrupted human nature. Wesleyan readers hold it in Article VII of the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church, and Wesleyan members differ in how they state the guilt; they hold also that Christ's work covers children who have not yet sinned (Confession of Faith, Article VI), and speak of regeneration as the renewal of man in righteousness and of believers as partakers of the divine nature (Confession of Faith, Article IX; 2 Peter 1:4, which the first reading also cites). Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 6) and the General Association of Regular Baptist Churches (Article VI) state the corruption of Adam's descendants and their guilt in him. The Foursquare Church's Declaration of Faith (Article III) states the corruption and guilt of Adam's descendants, and the Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (Statement 4) names death, physical and spiritual, through Adam without further definition. Most in these traditions speak of a person as body and soul, and some as body, soul and spirit.

passages.quote: For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.
passages.note: The sentence of death on Adam, read as passing to his descendants.

passages.quote: Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.
passages.note: “Because all sinned” read as all sharing in Adam's sin.

passages.quote: So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.
passages.note: One trespass, condemnation for all.

passages.quote: For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.
passages.note: The many made sinners through one man's disobedience.

passages.quote: Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.
passages.note: Read as sinfulness from the beginning of a person's life.

passages.quote: Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath.
passages.note: “By nature” read as a condition received at birth.

passages.quote: and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.
passages.note: Read as naming what the image consisted of and what Christ renews.

passages.quote: Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!
passages.note: Read by this reading as saying that those born of the fallen are not born clean. Job's lament is about human frailty; this is the reading's own use of it.

passages.quote: Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.
passages.note: Flesh is born of flesh, and spirit of the Spirit.

passages.quote: There is no one righteous, not even one. There is no one who understands, no one who seeks God. All have turned away
passages.note: No one righteous, no one who understands, no one who seeks God, all turned away.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Ezekiel 18:20 to address the guilt of each generation's own deeds in Israel and not the question of Adam's family. They take Romans 7:9 to describe Paul's own coming to see sin through the law, and Matthew 19:14 and Deuteronomy 1:39 to speak of God's mercy toward children, whatever their condition. They take 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12 to describe the whole person, and Matthew 10:28 to name the two parts. They take Ephesians 2:1 with 2:3 as the whole person dead in trespasses and by nature children of wrath, a state shared by all in Adam; the three-part reading takes it as the death of the spirit toward God. How far that death reaches into the will is left to the card on total depravity.

readings.label: One living person: soul, spirit, heart and body are the whole human being seen from different sides, and each person answers for his or her own sin
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take Genesis 2:7 to say that the man became a living being, not that a soul was placed in a body, and take “soul”, “spirit”, “heart” and “flesh” to name the whole person from different sides. Anabaptist readers hold that death and an inclination toward sin came to everyone through Adam while guilt belongs to a person's own sin, and that children are in God's care until they can answer for themselves; their members differ in how they put this. The Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995) says the sin of Adam and Eve affects all while each is held accountable for his or her own behavior (Article 7), says that infants and children are safe in the care of God, and uses the phrase “age of accountability” of baptism (Article 11); the Dordrecht Confession (1632, Article II) says death spread to all men, because all sinned (Romans 5:12). The Mennonite confession takes the image of God to belong to the whole person, made for relationship with God, with others and with creation, marred by sin and restored in Christ (Articles 6 and 7); it does not take up whether a person is two parts, three, or one. Many Baptist and free-church readers hold this account of the fall and call the time before answering the age of accountability. The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000, Article III) says that Adam's posterity inherit a nature and an environment inclined toward sin and that they become transgressors, and are under condemnation, as soon as they are capable of moral action; it does not say how many parts a person has. Baptists of the 1689 London Confession hold the imputation of Adam's sin described in the previous reading. Baptist members differ on whether a person is two parts, three, or one. Wesleyan members differ: some hold the inherited guilt described in the previous reading, and others join this reading in holding that Christ's work covers children.

passages.quote: Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being.
passages.note: The man himself is the living being: dust and breath together.

passages.quote: Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.
passages.note: Heart, soul, mind and strength read as the whole person loving God.

passages.quote: Therefore I urge you, brothers, on account of God's mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.
passages.note: The body offered as worship: the whole person given to God.

passages.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.
passages.note: The hope set on the body raised and not on a part released from it. The Greek word for “natural” is psychikos, formed from psyche, “soul”.

passages.quote: The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son.
passages.note: Read by holders of this reading as saying each person answers for his own sin.

passages.quote: Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died.
passages.note: Read as a time before a person is answerable.

passages.quote: Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.
passages.note: The kingdom said to belong to children.

passages.quote: death was passed on to all men, because all sinned
passages.note: Death passed on to all men, with the reason given as that all sinned.

passages.quote: through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners
passages.note: The many made sinners through one man's disobedience.

passages.quote: your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish
passages.note: The Father in heaven is not willing that any of the little ones perish.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take 1 Thessalonians 5:23 (“entire spirit, soul, and body”) to say “all of you” in the manner of Deuteronomy 6:5, and Hebrews 4:12 to describe the word reaching the deepest inner life. They take Matthew 10:28 to set what people can do against what God can do with the whole person, and members differ on whether 2 Corinthians 5:8 describes a person between death and resurrection. They take “because all sinned” in Romans 5:12 as each person's own sin, and Psalm 51:5 and Ephesians 2:3 as confessions of the sinful world around a person and of a lifelong inclination, not of guilt received at birth. They take “dead in your trespasses and sins” in Ephesians 2:1 as the death that sin brings to the person who sins, as in Romans 7:9, and not the death of one part.

readings.label: Body, soul and spirit: the spirit is the part made to meet God, cut off at the fall and made alive again in Christ
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take 1 Thessalonians 5:23 to name three distinct parts of a person, and Hebrews 4:12 to show soul and spirit as divisible, the spirit being that by which a person knows and worships God. Many who hold it read Adam's fall as the death of the spirit toward God, and the new birth as that spirit made alive. The Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths (Statement 4) names spiritual death, which it describes as separation from God, and does not state how many parts a person has. Baptist and free-church members differ, many holding two parts. The first reading notes that some early writers named three parts.

passages.quote: for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.
passages.note: Read as a death toward God that came on the day of the fall.

passages.quote: Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
passages.note: Spirit, soul and body named in one sentence.

passages.quote: Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow.
passages.note: Soul and spirit spoken of as divisible, as joints and marrow are.

passages.quote: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.
passages.note: The spirit praying while the mind does not.

passages.quote: And you were dead in your trespasses and sins,
passages.note: Read as the spirit's death toward God.

passages.quote: But if Christ is in you, your body is dead because of sin, yet your spirit is alive because of righteousness.
passages.note: Read as the believer's spirit alive through Christ's presence; the Greek says only “the spirit”, and other readers take it as the Holy Spirit.

passages.quote: The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children.
passages.note: The Spirit and the believer's spirit named together.

passages.quote: Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.
passages.note: Read as the spirit made alive in the new birth.

passages.quote: His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth
passages.note: God is Spirit, and worship is in spirit and in truth.

passages.quote: be transformed by the renewing of your mind
passages.note: Believers are told to be transformed by the renewing of the mind.

passages.quote: God, whom I serve with my spirit
passages.note: Paul says he serves God with his spirit.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Matthew 10:28 and Ecclesiastes 12:7 to use a short form that names the outer and the inner person, with “soul” standing for the inner life as a whole. They take Genesis 2:7 to give the breath of life and the soul in one act, and Mark 12:30 to list ways of loving God and not a count of parts. Holders of this reading who hold the account of the fall in the second or third reading take Romans 5, Psalm 51:5 and Ezekiel 18:20 as those readings do; this reading adds an account of what part of a person the fall touched.

terms.note: The Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Wesleyan term for the condition that comes from Adam's sin, and the term of the Church of England's Article IX (“Original or Birth-Sin”); each tradition states it in its own way, and Eastern Orthodox writers often use the term ancestral sin instead.

A term that Eastern Orthodox writers often use in place of original sin for what Adam's fall passed on. None of the Orthodox documents cited on this card uses it; the Orthodox Church in America page speaks of the first sin and says its consequences, chiefly death, pass to all while only Adam and Eve are guilty of it.
The Catholic term for the holiness and right relation with God that Adam was given before the fall.

A Reformed term for Adam standing for the human family, so that his act is counted as theirs. Reformed teaching sets this in the covenant of works made with Adam and his posterity (Westminster Confession 7.2, held by the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church).
The Eastern Orthodox term for a human being's growth in union with God, drawing on 2 Peter 1:4.
Genesis 1:26 uses two Hebrew words, tselem and demut. Some readers, early Christian writers among them, take them as two things; others take them as one thing said twice.
The scholarly names for the views that a person has two parts (body and soul) or three (body, soul and spirit); they are descriptions of a position and do not belong to one tradition.

English renders the Hebrew nephesh and ruach and the Greek psyche and pneuma; the words also mean life, breath, self and wind, and readers differ on how far they name parts. The Hebrew phrase translated “living being” in Genesis 2:7 is the one the Berean renders “living creatures” of the animals in Genesis 1:24; readers differ on what that shows.

The Greek words eph' ho at the end of Romans 5:12 have been rendered 'because', 'in whom' and 'with the result that'; readers differ partly on this, and the Berean's 'because' is one of the renderings.

A Baptist, free-church and Anabaptist phrase for the time before which a child is held not to answer for his or her own sin; the Mennonite confession (Article 11) uses it of baptism. The phrase is not found in the text.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 5, Decree on Original Sin, canons 1-5
further_reading.says: It teaches that Adam lost the holiness and justice he was given, that death and sin passed to his descendants by propagation and not by imitation, that infants are baptized for the remission of original sin, and that concupiscence remains in the baptized.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 355-384 (Man: the image of God; body and soul)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the human person is made in God's image, that body and soul form one nature, and that the distinction of soul and spirit in Scripture does not divide the soul into two parts (367).

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 385-421 (The Fall; original sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that Adam and Eve lost original holiness at once, that original sin is contracted and not committed, and that human nature is wounded and not wholly corrupted (399, 404-405).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decrees 6, 14 and 16
further_reading.says: Decree 6 says hereditary sin flowed to Adam's posterity and names the inherited burden as such punishments as toil, sickness and death, Decree 14 says the fallen kept free will, and Decree 16 says infants are subject to original sin.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 113-115 and 164-169
further_reading.says: It teaches that the image of God consists in righteousness and holiness of truth, that the soul is a spiritual and immortal substance, and that all who descend from Adam are born infected with sin and mortal.

further_reading.title: Orthodox Church in America, Questions and Answers: Original Sin
further_reading.says: A priest's reply on the Church's teaching pages, not an adopted statement: it says that everyone bears the consequences of the first sin, the foremost of which is death, and that only Adam and Eve are guilty of it.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article II (Of Original Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that all people born in the natural way after Adam's fall are born in sin, without fear of God and with concupiscence, and that this is truly sin.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration, Article I (Original Sin), paragraphs 9-14
further_reading.says: It teaches that original sin is a total lack of the original righteousness and of God's image, with a corruption of the whole nature, and that only a weakened understanding in outward matters remains.

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, The Creed, First Article
further_reading.says: It teaches that God has made me and all creatures and has given me my body and soul.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 4.2, chapter 6, chapter 7.2 and chapter 10.3
further_reading.says: It teaches that God made man with reasonable and immortal souls, endued with knowledge, righteousness and true holiness after his own image, that Adam's guilt was imputed and his nature corrupted in his descendants, that God made a covenant of works with Adam and his posterity, and that elect infants dying in infancy are saved.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 10, 16, 18 and 19
further_reading.says: It teaches that God made man in his image with knowledge, righteousness and holiness, that all mankind sinned in Adam, and that the sinfulness of the fallen estate is the guilt of Adam's first sin, the want of original righteousness and the corruption of the whole nature.

further_reading.title: Canons of Dort, First Head article 17; Third and Fourth Heads, articles 1-3
further_reading.says: Article I.17 tells believing parents not to doubt the election and salvation of children God takes in infancy, and III/IV articles 1-3 teach that people lost the knowledge, righteousness and purity of the image and pass a corrupted nature to their children.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 6-10
further_reading.says: It teaches that God made people good and in his own image, that the fall of Adam and Eve poisoned human nature so that everyone is conceived and born in a sinful condition, and that God is angry at both inherited and personal sin.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, chapter 15 (The state in which man was created; the image of God)
further_reading.says: Calvin treats the body formed from dust, the immortality of the soul, the faculties of the soul and the image of God in man's original state.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 2, chapter 1 (Through the fall of Adam the whole human race made accursed and degenerate; of original sin)
further_reading.says: Calvin teaches that original sin is transmitted by propagation and not imitation, and defines it as a hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Article IX (Of Original or Birth-Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that original sin is not the following of Adam but the corruption of the nature of every man, which remains even in the regenerate, and that there is no condemnation for them that believe and are baptized.

further_reading.title: To Be a Christian: An Anglican Catechism (2019), question 46
further_reading.says: The catechism says that I have inherited this fallen and corrupted human nature.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Articles II and VII
further_reading.says: Article VII rejects the view that original sin is following Adam and teaches the corruption of the nature of every man, very far gone from original righteousness, and Article II speaks of Christ's sacrifice for original guilt as well as actual sins.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church, Articles VI, VII and IX
further_reading.says: Article VI says children are under the atonement of Christ, Article VII says man is fallen from righteousness, and Article IX speaks of regeneration as the renewal of man in righteousness and of believers as partakers of the divine nature.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 44 (Original Sin)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that through Adam all became sinners and lost the life and the image of God, and that human nature is corrupted in every faculty and needs healing.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 45 (The New Birth)
further_reading.says: Wesley distinguishes a natural, a political and a moral image of God in man, teaches that the fall brought spiritual death and the loss of the moral image, and describes the new birth as its renewal.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article III (Man)
further_reading.says: It teaches that man is made in God's image with full dignity, that his posterity inherit a nature and an environment inclined toward sin, and that they become transgressors under condemnation as soon as they are capable of moral action.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 6 (Of the Fall of Man, of Sin, and of the Punishment Thereof)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 3 teaches that our first parents stood for all their descendants, so that the guilt of their sin was imputed and a corrupted nature conveyed to them by natural birth.

further_reading.body: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
further_reading.title: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches, Articles of Faith, Article VI (The Fall of Mankind)
further_reading.says: It teaches that all human beings sinned in Adam, are partakers of his fallen nature, and are under just condemnation.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Statement 4 (The Fall of Man)
further_reading.says: Statement 4 says that man by voluntary transgression fell and incurred not only physical death but also spiritual death, which is separation from God.

further_reading.title: Foursquare Declaration of Faith, Article III (The Fall of Man)
further_reading.says: Article III says that in consequence of Adam's disobedience all mankind are sinners, without by nature the holiness the law of God requires, positively inclined to evil, and guilty and without excuse.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 6 (Creation and Calling of Human Beings)
further_reading.says: It teaches that human beings are made in God's image, that the image refers to the whole person, and that people are made for relationship with God, with one another and with creation.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 7 (Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the sin of Adam and Eve affects all, that sin marred the image of God, and that each person is held accountable for his or her own behavior.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 11 (Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is for those who are of the age of accountability, and that infants and children are safe in the care of God.

further_reading.title: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), Article II (Of the Fall of Man)
further_reading.says: It teaches that Adam and Eve disobeyed after the serpent's deceit, and that death spread to all men, because all sinned (Romans 5:12).

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Reading 1 answers: Hebrews 4:12 no longer counted among the verses that name three
_review_2026_10_25.why: Hebrews 4:12 names soul and spirit, not three; 1 Thessalonians 5:23 is the verse that names three.

_review_2026_10_25.fix: Reading 4 summary: Hebrews 4:12 shown as soul and spirit divisible; vague 'several other traditions' sentence replaced by a pointer to the first reading

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked: Gen 1:26 (clause 'Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness' without the opening curly mark), 1:27, 1:31 (first clause), 2:7, 2:17 (second clause, trailing mark omitted), 3:19 (last sentence, trailing mark omitted), 9:6 (clause), Job 14:4, Ps 51:5, Ezek 18:20 (first two sentences), Matt 10:28, 19:14 (the quoted words without the opening mark), Mark 12:30 (server ends with a stray mark after the period, omitted), John 3:6, Rom 3:23, 5:12, 5:18, 5:19, 7:9, 8:10, 8:16, 12:1, 1 Cor 14:14, 15:22, 15:44 (first sentence), 15:49, 2 Cor 5:8, Eph 2:1, 2:3 (second sentence), 4:24, Col 1:15, 3:10, 1 Thess 5:23, Heb 4:12 (second sentence), Jas 3:9, 2 Pet 1:4 (clause). All ticked. Nothing quoted from Ps 8, Gen 3 beyond 3:19, Rom 7:18 or Gen 6:5 and 8:21: those are about how far sin reaches into the will and are kept for total-depravity. SHAPE: this question joins three things that are asked separately (what a person is made of, what the image is, what the fall changed). The traditions do not line up behind one answer on all three, so the four readings are bundles, each with the account of parts and of the fall that its holders usually put together. The cost of the bundles is that held_by is approximate, and the summaries say where members differ. ORDER: by when each reading was first stated as a settled position by the traditions that hold it, as I read the history, and it does not rank them. First the early church and its heirs (Catholic and Orthodox); second the Reformation statements (1500s onward, building on the earlier Western teaching of Adam's sin); third the Anabaptist (1520s) and later Baptist readings; fourth the three-part reading as a held position in the 1800s and 1900s, although three-part language is in some early writers and is noted in reading 1. PASSAGES: 8, 8, 7 and 8 in the readings and 8 in the common ground; duplicates across readings are intended (Rom 5:12 in readings 1 and 2; Eph 4:24 in readings 1 and 2; Gen 2:7 in the common ground and in reading 3), each with its own note. LEFT OUT: total depravity, inability and the bondage of the will (for the total-depravity card); the intermediate state and soul sleep; the creation of Eve and the roles of the sexes; whether the image is reason, rule, relation or a calling (a gap that cuts across all four readings and may want a card of its own); the Jewish reading of Genesis 1:26-27, 9:6 and Ezekiel 18, which holds a person born without an inherited guilt and speaks of two inclinations, not among the traditions credited and not added. See _review_2026_10_25 for the changes made after the panel.
